articles.title: Your iPhone may die faster this week: Here’s why
articles.summary: As annoying as it may be, it should be short-lived.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) — The latest major update from Apple, iOS 27, was released to qualifying devices on Monday, bringing with it a slew of improvements and new features to iPhones, iPads, and more.

This marks the second major iOS update in Apple’s new naming system. Last year, Apple broke from the numerical pattern it had been following, naming the annual update iOS 26 rather than the expected iOS 19.

But, like all system updates before it, iOS 27 is massive, requiring several gigabytes of space on your iPhone or other Apple devices. A lack of space may be one of a handful of obstacles standing between you and the newest Apple features.

Once you are able to download iOS 27 on your iPhone or iPad, you may notice yourself reaching for the charger more frequently than you were last week.

Apple has previously warned that major iOS updates can temporarily have a negative impact on your device’s battery life.

“Immediately after completing an update, particularly a major release, you might notice a temporary impact on battery life and thermal performance,” the company says on a support page . “This is normal, as your device needs time to complete the setup process in the background, including indexing data and files for search, downloading new assets, and updating apps.”

It typically lasts for only a few days while your device continues behind-the-scenes work. However, Apple also warns that your use of your iPhone or iPad will continue to have an impact on the battery. If you’re exploring the new features from iOS 27, you may be a contributing factor in your device dying more quickly.

It is also recommended that you do not allow your iPhone to charge to 100% during these draining times. Experts and phone manufacturers generally advise charging only to 80% to prolong the battery life.

articles.title: Scammers know the best time to text you
articles.summary: Malwarebytes data reveals scam texts peak around noon ET with 874% higher volume than overnight, and Fridays bring roughly 50% more messages.
articles.body: If your phone seems to light up with suspicious texts right when your day gets busy, you may not be imagining it. New research from cybersecurity company Malwarebytes suggests scammers have gotten much more strategic about when they contact you and where they do it. The company analyzed global threat data collected between April 15 and July 14, 2026. Researchers tracked more than 20 scam categories. They found that criminals often choose the platform that gives a particular scam the best chance of working. Then there is the timing. For Americans, scam text volume peaked around 12 p.m. ET. That was about 874% higher than at 1 a.m. ET, the quietest hour Malwarebytes observed. Scam text volume also climbed as the week went on. It reached its highest point on Friday, when people received roughly 50% more fraudulent texts than at the beginning of the week. That tells me scammers are paying attention to more than what they send you. They are also watching when you may be most likely to see it. And the timing is only part of the strategy, because the type of scam often determines exactly where they try to reach you. THE SCAM TEXT TEST: SPOT DANGER BEFORE YOU TAP NEW! Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you take a more active role in your healthcare. You’ll learn how to organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare questions for your next doctor’s visit. No technical experience is needed. Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com. Scammers are choosing the best place to reach you Different scams tend to favor different platforms. Malwarebytes found that job scams commonly arrive through email. Romance scams favor social media, where conversations with new people feel more natural. Meanwhile, tech support scams frequently start with a phone call. That makes sense when you think about how each scam works. A fake recruiter can blend into a busy inbox. Someone starting a conversation on social media may seem harmless. A caller claiming your computer has a serious problem can immediately put you under pressure. The channel becomes part of the trick. We've seen that with changing tech support scams. They can now begin with fake invoices, bogus security alerts or convincing support pages. The web remains scammers' favorite doorway You hear plenty about scam texts and suspicious DMs. However, the web remains the leading way scams reach people in Malwarebytes' data. Email came next, followed by SMS. Malwarebytes says it blocks around 500,000 phishing websites every day. That number gives you an idea of how many fake pages criminals keep pushing online. Some copy banks or popular retailers. Others imitate technology companies or government services. A link in a text can take you straight to one of these pages. The fake site may look polished enough to fool you at first glance. So, when a message says something has gone wrong with an account, resist the urge to use the link it provides. Open the company's app yourself or type the website address directly into your browser. Scam texts hit their peak around lunchtime Here's the part that really caught my attention. Malwarebytes found that scam texts targeting Americans reached their highest volume around 12 p.m. ET. At noon, volume was about 874% higher than at 1 a.m. ET. Think about what your phone habits look like around lunchtime. You could be leaving a meeting, grabbing something to eat or checking messages between errands. Your attention may already be split. Then a text arrives saying your package cannot be delivered. Another claims you owe a toll. Maybe a message warns that somebody accessed your account. That timing can work in a scammer's favor because you may react before giving the message a closer look. Of course, a text arriving at noon does not automatically mean somebody is trying to scam you. The data shows when Malwarebytes observed the highest volume. Still, the pattern gives us another look at how organized scam campaigns have become. IS THAT TRAFFIC TICKET TEXT A SCAM OR REAL? Fridays bring even more scam texts The day of the week also appears to play a role. Malwarebytes saw its lowest scam text volume on Sunday. Activity then increased as the week went on. By Friday, people were receiving roughly 50% more fraudulent texts than at the beginning of the week. The researchers cannot say exactly why Friday produced the highest volume. However, the pattern suggests scammers may be deliberately timing campaigns instead of sending messages at random. Maybe you're finishing work and thinking about the weekend. You could also be juggling deliveries, travel plans or bills. Whatever the reason, criminals want you moving quickly. That's something we've seen repeatedly with fake government messages. A DMV scam text can threaten fines or license problems while pushing you toward a payment page. The threat gets your attention. The deadline tries to stop you from thinking. MrBeast is the most impersonated person in the data Timing gets the message in front of you. Familiarity can make you trust it. Malwarebytes found that Jimmy Donaldson, better known as MrBeast, was the most impersonated person in its data. His likeness appeared in about 30% of impersonation scams observed by the company. Elon Musk and Donald Trump followed him in the data. These scams can involve fake cryptocurrency giveaways or schemes that demand a fee before you supposedly receive money. The real person has nothing to do with the offer. Scammers borrow a face you recognize because familiarity can lower your guard. That tactic has become even more troubling as AI-generated video and cloned voices improve. A face on your screen no longer proves the person actually made the video. Google leads the list of impersonated brands Scammers use the same strategy with companies you recognize. According to reports from Malwarebytes users, the five most impersonated brands were: Google, Microsoft, Apple, Roblox and Amazon. Google's name appeared at least twice as often as Amazon's. That familiarity gives criminals a huge advantage. If you use Google every day, a fake security warning may look routine. An Apple customer may react quickly to a message about an account problem. Amazon scams can land at exactly the right moment because so many of us regularly have packages on the way. So, treat the logo as decoration until you verify the message yourself. Gaming scams are getting more attention Gaming communities are also attracting scammers. Malwarebytes found Roblox, Steam, Discord and Minecraft among the most impersonated gaming platforms. Roblox scam activity increased 15% between mid-June and mid-July. Steam saw a 19% increase during the same period. The potential losses can also get serious. Malwarebytes says about half of the gaming scams it analyzed could lead to losses of $1,000 or more. That is particularly concerning when younger gamers may encounter fake offers through communities they already trust. A message promising free in-game items or access to something exclusive can quickly lead to a fake login page. Once the victim enters a password, the scammer may take over the account. AMAZON JOB SCAM TEXTS ARE SPREADING AGAIN WITH A NEW TWIST How to protect yourself from better-timed scams Scammers can improve their timing, but you can make yourself a much harder target. The best defense starts with slowing down and verifying what you see. 1) Don't click links or call numbers in unexpected messages Avoid links and phone numbers inside unsolicited emails, texts or social media messages. A link can take you to a copied website designed to steal your login or payment information. Likewise, the phone number in a fake security alert can connect you directly to the scammer. Instead, leave the message and contact the company another way. 2) Verify the message through an official source Go directly to the company's official website or open its app. If the message claims you owe money, check your real account before paying anything. You can also contact the organization using a phone number you already trust. This breaks the scammer's control over the conversation. 3) Be careful with sponsored search results Searching for a company's website can help, but pay close attention to what you click. Scammers can use sponsored search ads that lead to fake support pages or convincing copies of legitimate websites. Check the web address before entering sensitive information. When possible, use a saved bookmark or the company's official app. 4) Keep passwords and verification codes private Never give someone your password because they called or messaged you unexpectedly. The same goes for PINs, account recovery codes and one-time verification codes. A scammer may claim they need a code to verify your identity. In reality, that code may give them access to your account. If a caller asks for sensitive information, hang up and contact the organization yourself. 5) Never send payment because someone pressures you Be suspicious when an unexpected caller or message demands immediate payment. Before paying, confirm the charge through your actual account or by contacting the organization independently. Watch closely for payment requests involving gift cards, cryptocurrency or transfers that may be difficult to reverse. Urgency should make you more cautious, not less. 6) Use browser protection against scam sites Strong antivirus software can help block known phishing sites and other malicious pages. Browser protection can also warn you before you enter information on a dangerous website. Keep your browser updated as well. Security updates help close weaknesses that criminals may try to exploit. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. 7) Turn on scam and spam filtering on your phone Your phone may already include tools that identify suspicious calls or messages. Turn on spam filtering when your device and messaging app support it. Mobile security software can provide another layer of protection by identifying scam texts and dangerous links. No filter catches everything, so continue checking unexpected messages yourself. 8) Check suspicious messages before responding If something feels wrong, look into it before you reply. Search for the company's official contact information. Check your account directly. You can also use a reputable scam-checking service to examine a suspicious phone number, message or link. The goal is simple. Verify the claim somewhere outside the conversation the scammer started. 9) Block and report scam messages Once you know a message is fraudulent, block the sender and report it as spam. Most phones and email services include built-in reporting options. Reporting scams can also help providers identify campaigns and block similar messages for other users. Then delete the message so you do not accidentally interact with it later. Act quickly if you already clicked or shared information If you entered a password on a suspicious site, change it immediately using the real website or app. Change that password anywhere else you reused it. Better yet, use a password manager to create and store strong, unique passwords for each account so one stolen password cannot unlock several accounts. If you gave away payment information, contact your bank or card issuer right away. You should also review your accounts for unfamiliar activity. If a scammer gained access to your device, disconnect it from the internet and run a trusted security scan. Kurt's key takeaways What grabs me about this research is how deliberate scam campaigns are becoming. Scammers are paying attention to where you spend your time. Now, the timing data suggests they may also be watching when you're more likely to respond. That changes how I think about those random-looking texts that pop up during a busy day. The message may feel like one more thing that needs your attention. That's exactly when you need to slow down. You cannot control when a scammer contacts you. You can control whether that person gets to set the pace. When something unexpected asks for money or account information, get out of the message. Find the real company on your own and check the claim there. That small pause can ruin a scammer's entire plan. Have you noticed more scam texts arriving around lunchtime or toward the end of the week, and what kind of message almost fooled you into responding? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. articles.title: Carney Says US Deal Possible, Blow-Up Helped Clarify ‘Red Lines’
articles.summary: The dramatic collapse of trade talks with the US in August helped clarify Canada’s negotiating “red lines,” said Prime Minister Mark Carney, who added he’s r...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The dramatic collapse of trade talks with the US in August helped clarify Canada's negotiating "red lines," said Prime Minister Mark Carney, who added he's ready to get back to the table for the right deal.

In an interview with Bloomberg News, he was asked whether it's a question of who moves first to get negotiations restarted.

"There's not a pride thing from our perspective," he said. "We're practical people that know what our bottom lines are, what our red lines are for sovereignty, for culture, not being restricted on our ability to sign other trade deals."

The prime minister added: "I think our American colleagues maybe, perhaps, understand those red lines a little more clearly now, given what's happened. We're ready to sit down."

But Canada is "not going to slow down" on its efforts to expand trade with other countries, said Carney, who has invited the world's leading money managers to Toronto this week for the inaugural Canada Investment Summit — a bid to pull in more foreign direct investment. As soon as it ends, he'll fly to France for talks on deepening Canada's relationship with the European Union.

Top-level discussions between the US and Canada fell apart on Aug. 21 over a deal that would have reduced US tariffs on core Canadian sectors like steel and automotive, while eliminating a number of Canadian trade restrictions.

The next day, President Donald Trump's administration implemented 50% tariffs against about $20 billion of Canadian exports. Canada has retaliated with counter-tariffs hitting the same total dollar value of US exports.

Both sides blamed each other for the blow-up and claimed each had made last-minute demands. Carney said the US wanted to infringe on Canadian cultural protections around the French language and restrict Canada's ability to sign other trade deals.

Despite this, on Saturday, Trump said a deal with Canada could come "fairly soon," without elaborating.

Carney said he welcomed those comments and added Canada's ready to sit down for a deal that respects each side's sovereignty and Canada's cultural institutions.

"We'll sit down when it makes sense. Canada and the US have a very long relationship. We sometimes go through periods where there are tensions in that relationship. Provided we continue this approach, we'll come to some some agreement at some point."

articles.title: Ballmer apologizes as Clippers accept $30M salary cap circumvention fine
articles.summary: Billionaire owner Steve Ballmer has apologized for his role in an effort by the Los Angeles Clippers to circumvent the NBA’s salary cap by funneling money to star player Kawhi Leonard through endorsement opportunities. “This has been a very difficult time for everybody associated with the Clippers, and for that, I have sincere regrets,” Ballmer…
articles.body:
Billionaire owner Steve Ballmer has apologized for his role in an effort by the Los Angeles Clippers to circumvent the NBA’s salary cap by funneling money to star player Kawhi Leonard through endorsement opportunities.

“This has been a very difficult time for everybody associated with the Clippers, and for that, I have sincere regrets,” Ballmer said in a statement issued late Sunday night. “I want to apologize to our fans, employees, and my fellow NBA team owners for the distraction and distress this matter has caused, for which I accept responsibility as principal owner.”

The Clippers were docked five draft picks and fined $30 million earlier this month, and Ballmer was banned for a year from basketball activities as punishment for the scheme.

The club initially pushed back on the NBA’s punishment, among the steepest handed down to a team in the league’s history, calling it “the result of a heavily biased investigation seeking to justify a predetermined narrative rather than facts and evidence.”

Ballmer took a softer tone in his Sunday statement.

“We are committing to put this chapter behind us. We have communicated to the NBA that we are complying with the penalties assessed by the league, have paid the fine, and are moving forward,” the former Microsoft executive and one of the NBA’s richest owners said. “While there are still disagreements concerning the findings in the report, this is not where I want to focus. Team owners should support, not distract.”

The Clippers owner’s apology comes amid reports President Trump’s Department of Justice is investigating the club in connection with the Leonard scandal, though it is unclear whether Ballmer or Leonard are the subject of the criminal probe.

articles.title: AI leaders call for development slowdown
articles.summary: A growing chorus of artificial intelligence leaders are calling for a slowdown of the technology’s development following a researcher’s ominous warning that AI could soon destroy humanity. Shortly after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called to slow down AI capability development, several of his competitors, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI CEO Elon Musk, followed…
articles.body:
A growing chorus of artificial intelligence leaders are calling for a slowdown of the technology’s development following a researcher’s ominous warning that AI could soon destroy humanity.

Shortly after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called to slow down AI capability development , several of his competitors, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI CEO Elon Musk, followed suit.

The calls followed a post from 27-year-old AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who claimed researchers at the firms “believe AI could kill all humans” but still push forward in a race to develop superintelligence — a hypothetical AI agent that outperforms all of humanity’s cognitive performance. Coxon resigned from Anthropic before sharing his warnings on social media.

In a lengthy post on X , Altman said the “world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especially as the trajectory of progress has steepened.”

“Every frontier lab must deliver on this, and there is no reason any of us should come to work if we cannot,” Altman said.

Altman reiterated OpenAI’s support of a federal framework for safety requirements, but also argued the industry does not need to wait for legislation or an antitrust exemption to create “consistent rules” and shared values along the firms.

Altman said pacing development does not mean stopping, but that development “should be slower than it otherwise could be.”

“Pacing will be well worth this cost; no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness, or let capabilities get ahead of alignment and monitoring,” Altman said.

Musk, who originally co-founded OpenAI with Altman, reposted Amodei as well, writing that “Dario is right.”

The comments mark a shift for AI leaders, who have shied away from any commitments to slow down until recently.

Researchers have warned of AI’s potential danger for years, but nothing struck a chord quite like Coxon’s social media thread.

Coxon’s assessment went viral with more than 165 million views and within a few hours, the debate over the long-term implications of artificial intelligence was no longer confined within the technology community.

Coxon is among a camp of what critics dubbed AI “doomers,” who believe the technology will lead to mass extinction if development is not safety-aligned or slowed down.

“These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources,” Coxon wrote on social media. “We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing.”

Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, affirmed Coxon’s warning, stating, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans !”

articles.title: Trump says Russia, Ukraine agree to avoid energy targets as fuel prices rise
articles.summary: President Trump said Monday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to avoid energy targets in their ongoing war as global fuel prices rise. “Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do likewise!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. The post comes as both gasoline and diesel prices are rising worldwide.…
articles.body:
President Trump said Monday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to avoid energy targets in their ongoing war as global fuel prices rise.

“Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do likewise!” Trump wrote on Truth Social .

The post comes as both gasoline and diesel prices are rising worldwide. Refining capacity shortages are a factor in the high prices, as global conflicts take out refineries.

U.S. diesel prices recently crossed $6 per gallon for the first time ever and averaged $6.23 per gallon on Monday, according to AAA. Gasoline prices averaged about $4.32 per gallon.

The high prices have created issues for the White House going into the midterms. Trump, in his post, sought to distance his administration and its decision to go to war with Iran from the issue.

“The World’s Diesel price rise is mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine War, not Iran,” he said.

In a social media post of his own , Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said his nation “is not convinced that Russia is willing to abide by any agreement.”

“If our partners are ready to ensure that Russia genuinely refrains from striking our electricity system, other energy facilities, critical infrastructure, and food supply routes, then, of course, we are ready to ensure a corresponding halt to our strikes,” Zelensky wrote, adding, “We expect specifics from our partners.”

Experts have said that the Russia-Ukraine conflict is playing a part, but it’s not the only thing driving up prices, as Middle East instability is also factor.

“Average gasoline and diesel prices rose in every state over the last week as geopolitical tensions escalated on multiple fronts, with friction between the U.S. and Iran, new hostilities in the Red Sea, and the shutdown of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline all combining to jolt prices sharply higher,” said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy in a statement posted online . “New weekend attacks also knocked two additional Russian refineries offline, further straining global refined product supplies and likely offsetting any seasonal relief.”

Laura Kelly contributed. Updated at 12:38 p.m. EDT

articles.title: States and cities sue over ‘public charge’ green card restrictions
articles.summary: A coalition of Democratic-led states and Washington, D.C., are suing the Trump administration to block a rule that makes it harder for immigrants to obtain green cards or even enter the country if they rely on public benefits. The 22 states and D.C. are challenging the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) “public charge” rule, set…
articles.body:
A coalition of Democratic-led states and Washington, D.C., are suing the Trump administration to block a rule that makes it harder for immigrants to obtain green cards or even enter the country if they rely on public benefits.

The 22 states and D.C. are challenging the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) “public charge” rule , set to take effect Friday.

The states, led by New York Attorney General Letitia James (D), argue the rule will penalize immigrants and their families for using public benefits like food stamps, Medicaid or housing vouchers to which they are legally entitled.

“Hardworking families should not be forced to go without the support they need because they fear asking for assistance will get them deported,” James said in a statement. “This rule preys on that fear and counts on families forfeiting the food assistance, health care coverage, and other public benefits to which they are legally entitled.”

The lawsuit argues that under the rule, immigrants would need to stop using public assistance programs to meet their basic needs or risk being denied green cards in the future.

Noncitizens and family members would disenroll from programs, even though they are eligible, and the states argued they will lose billions of dollars in federal funding.

They said the rule is “arbitrary and capricious” and that the DHS both ignored the harmful consequences of the change and failed to adequately justify it.

“As households forgo their legal access to benefits—such as preventative healthcare, nutritional assistance, and school lunch—public health, local economies, public education, and public safety will suffer. The Final Rule will increase the prevalence of disease, drive up the costs of medical care, and increase poverty,” the lawsuit argued.

A separate lawsuit challenging the rule was filed by a group of local governments, led by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D).

The Trump administration argues the rule is necessary to protect American taxpayers from subsidizing immigrants who may become dependent on public benefits.

The law focuses only on immigrants who are lawfully present and eligible to apply for permanent residency. Immigrants who are in the country illegally are not eligible for public benefits.

The final rule is a revival of a similar policy that the administration tried to impose during President Trump’s first term before it was met with legal challenges and later reversed by the Biden administration.

So-called “public charge” restrictions that bar immigrants from obtaining green cards if they are likely to rely on government assistance have been part of federal immigration policy for more than 140 years, but they have long focused only on cash benefit programs.

The Trump administration’s first attempt to change the rule broadened the types of benefits to include the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, most Medicaid benefits and certain housing programs.

The new rule has no limits of what can be considered, saying only the DHS “will consider the receipt of any means tested public benefits.”

For example, if a U.S. citizen child uses state-provided health insurance, that can be used against a noncitizen parent to deny them a green card. Officers could also count a child’s participation in a school’s free lunch program against their noncitizen parent’s application for citizenship.

“The final rule puts families in the untenable position of choosing between a U.S. citizen child’s access to healthcare, and their noncitizen parent’s ability to remain in the country,” the lawsuit argued.

The states’ suit was brought by the attorneys general of California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Nevada, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, along with the governor of Pennsylvania.

Alongside New York City, the local lawsuit was brought by Chicago; the City and County of San Francisco; Santa Clara County, Calif.; Seattle; and King County, Wash.

articles.title: GLP-1-driven vitamin deficiency linked to rare brain disorder: Study
articles.summary: Researchers found a rare but potentially life-threatening brain disorder in a small number of people taking Ozempic, Wegovy and similar drugs.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — A new study found that a rare but serious brain condition has been identified in a small number of people taking popular weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro and Zepbound.

Wernicke encephalopathy is a rare neurological disorder caused by a severe deficiency of vitamin B1, also known as thiamine.

Researchers identified 15 cases reported in 2023 and 2024 among people taking GLP-1 medications containing semaglutide, found in Ozempic and Wegovy, or tirzepatide, found in Mounjaro and Zepbound.

Vitamin B1 is essential for proper nerve function. Without enough of it, patients can develop confusion, problems with balance and coordination, and abnormal eye movements.

If left untreated, the condition can lead to permanent brain damage or death. Physicians consider it a medical emergency.

GLP-1 drugs can contribute to vitamin deficiencies by suppressing appetite and reducing food intake, including foods rich in vitamin B1, such as pork, fish and whole grains.

The study found that most patients who developed the condition also experienced severe vomiting, loss of appetite, poor nutrition or rapid weight loss.

While the disorder remains rare, researchers said the findings should help doctors educate patients about the risk and monitor for warning signs.

articles.title: Brothers rescue group of elderly people from burning California assisted living facility
articles.summary: (KTLA) — Two young brothers worked quickly to rescue a group of elderly people after a fire broke out at an assisted living facility in Glendale, Calif., on Friday. Glendale firefighters responded to the burning home on the 1800 block of Mountain Street around 4:45 p.m. As the flames grew and heavy smoke billowed from…
articles.body:
( KTLA ) — Two young brothers worked quickly to rescue a group of elderly people after a fire broke out at an assisted living facility in Glendale, Calif., on Friday.

Glendale firefighters responded to the burning home on the 1800 block of Mountain Street around 4:45 p.m.

As the flames grew and heavy smoke billowed from the home, neighbors Alex Bazinyan, 20, and his brother Narek Bazinyan, 15, realized time was of the essence and decided to run over and help.

“I ran outside and I was looking at the front door when I saw the nurse outside and she was screaming for help,” Alex told Nexstar’s KTLA’s John Fenoglio.

The brothers knew several people were trapped inside the home that was operating as an assisted living facility for seniors.

Narek initially grabbed a garden hose to help quell the flames, but as the blaze grew more intense and screams for help grew louder, they knew they had to run into the fire.

“I go inside this big room and I see all these old people on the floor with catheters,” Alex recalled. “Some people were injured, had blood on their legs. We just took everybody out one by one.”

There were eight people inside the home — two nurses and six elderly residents, most of whom were unable to walk. The brothers said the nurses were desperately trying to remove the elderly residents from the home but were struggling.

“I see a guy in the back about to be engulfed by the flames,” Narek recalled when he entered the home. “The nurse is trying to pick him up. I go and grab his legs and pull him out to the front.”

Soon after, two additional neighbors also ran over to help evacuate the residents.

“As I’m looking around, I just see flames going up and coming towards me,” Narek said. “I tried bringing everyone out as fast as I could. There was smoke everywhere. I was pretty much blinded by the smoke.”

The brothers were able to safely rescue all six elderly residents and placed them on the front lawn as they awaited fire crews.

But just as they moved the last person out of the burning home, Alex recalled hearing a loud explosion.

“I heard an explosion come from the house,” he said. “I looked back and I didn’t understand what exploded, but I just heard a big boom.”

Firefighters arrived at the home and were able to extinguish the flames before any nearby houses were affected. The Glendale Fire Department chief said an oxygen tank likely exploded, which collapsed part of the home.

Seven people were transported to the hospital with minor injuries. The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

As for Alex and Narek, they said their instincts just kicked in and the only thing they were focused on was quickly rescuing everyone from the burning home.

“It’s that instinct of whenever you see people in need, you want to help them out,” Alex said. “You don’t really think about who it is. We have a really tight-knit community here.”

Narek agreed, saying, “If you ever see anyone in need, you should always try to help them out as much as you can.”

images.caption: Brothers Alex and Narek Bazinyan rescued six elderly people from a burning Glendale assisted living facility on Sept. 11, 2026. (KTLA/Citizen)

articles.title: ClickFix attacks are tricking Mac and Windows users into hacking themselves | TechCrunch
articles.summary: If you clicked on a fake HBO Max ad on Reddit in the past week, you might have fallen victim to a rising "ClickFix" security threat.
articles.body:
If you clicked on an HBO Max ad on Reddit over the past week, you might want to check your computer for malware.

These so-called “ClickFix” attacks have quickly become one of the rising cybersecurity threats of 2026, and they’re getting both sneakier and compromising people’s devices with greater frequency. Until recently, ClickFix attacks were a rarity, capitalizing on people searching the web for quick tech fixes. They have since evolved into a massive international effort to hack into people’s computers.

The attacks involve fake websites, or legitimate websites that have been hacked, which display a message that appears to look like a CAPTCHA or an anti-bot checkbox. Once clicked, a prompt appears asking the user to perform a “check” to proceed, which gives instructions to copy and paste a string of text into the user’s Windows command prompt or Mac Terminal app.

As soon as the user hits return, they unwittingly and instantly install info-stealing malware on their computer, capable of immediately stealing their passwords, access to their logged-in accounts, and crypto wallets. Since the user is working in the computer’s terminal, which lets them interact directly with the operating system using text-based commands, many of these attacks evade antivirus and security defense tools.

Security researchers now say that the latest ClickFix campaign they’ve seen involved hackers posting fake ads on Reddit, linking to a page that looks like HBO Max but contains a ClickFix lure that tricks people into hacking themselves. The hackers compromised the official HBO Max’s account on Reddit that was then used to post hundreds of fake but real-looking adverts to the news-sharing site, according to security researchers at Hudson Rock and a thread on Reddit’s cybersecurity subreddit.

It’s unclear how many people clicked on these fake ads or how many were ultimately compromised as a result. Warner Brothers Discovery, which owns HBO, did not respond to a request for comment.

Reddit told TechCrunch it “recently learned that an HBO Max account authorized to run advertisements on Reddit was compromised and used to run ads containing malicious links,” and that the company locked the account and removed the ads. When asked, Reddit did not say how many users were targeted or clicked the malicious ads.

While it’s typical for developers to run one-line snippets of code in their computer’s terminal, it’s less common for regular users to use the Command Prompt or PowerShell in Windows, or the Terminal in macOS. Companies that run fleets of Windows computers can block access to these features across the entire domain to prevent them from being exploited, per security researcher Kevin Beaumont .

As noted by Ars Technica , a tool for Mac users called BlockBlock can also defend against attacks that try to trick Apple users into hacking themselves.

articles.title: Florida’s ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ confined migrants in ‘small metal enclosures’: DHS internal watchdog

articles.body:
A new report reviewing the conditions at the now-closed “Alligator Alcatraz” center in Florida slammed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for failing to meet a variety of federal standards, describing “unprecedented” treatment of migrants, including containing them in cages about the size of a phone booth.

The Monday report from the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Office of Inspector General (OIG) is the first such federal review of the facility, which is referred to in the report as the Florida Soft-Sided Facility (FSSF).

The report describes alarming conditions, including unhygienic practices for food and water as well as limited opportunities for migrants to bathe themselves.

OIG said Alligator Alcatraz provided half the living space for migrants required under federal law — just 28 square feet when the facility was at max capacity, far from the 75-square-foot mandate.

ICE officials also used cages that were roughly 4 feet by 4 feet as “‘calming areas’ for detainees to deescalate and have time alone.”

“FSSF confined 79 detainees in small metal enclosures — each offering about 18 square feet of floor space — for periods ranging from several minutes to nearly 2 hours, a practice unlike any OIG team has observed in ICE facilities. The use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment,” OIG wrote.

OIG found that in at least one documented case, a migrant was put in the small cages as a punishment.

The report generated swift blowback from immigration advocates who targeted ICE’s explanation for the small cages.

“There is no euphemism that can sanitize caging human beings. Calling a metal box a ‘calming area’ is an affront to the English language and to human dignity alike,” Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, president and CEO of refugee settlement agency Global Refuge, said in a statement.

“The stark reality is that human beings, many of whom came to this country seeking protection, were crammed into spaces unfit to accommodate them, denied adequate medical care, food, and basic hygiene — and in at least one case locked in a cage as punishment. That is not immigration enforcement. It is cruelty, carried out in our name and on our dime, to the tune of more than a million dollars a day.”

OIG said they were unable to “independently confirm or refute ICE officials’ assertions regarding their use of the enclosures” as well as other allegations, such as deprivation of food or water issues described in a prior Amnesty International report, as none of the detainees interviewed while OIG was there reported those conditions.

“Use of these small metal enclosures for any reason is unprecedented among ICE facilities inspected by OIG. Confining individuals in small metal enclosures for any reason presents significant risks to detainee health and well-being,” the watchdog wrote.

Both ICE and DHS did not immediately respond to request for comment.

In the report, however, the agency and department placed much of the responsibility for the facility on Florida, despite it being constructed with federal funds and managed by ICE agents.

“While FEMA [Federal Emergency Management Agency] provided funding for the Florida Soft-Sided Facility (FSSF) under the Shelter and Services Program, DHS did not have a contract with Florida to manage the detention space within the facility. The State of Florida authorized the repurposing of the center from the Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport into a state detention center,” DHS officials wrote in a letter in response to the report.

Other aspects also generated significant attention from inspectors.

Several detainees told OIG investigators they did not have access to clean water, saying that self-serve water stations were dirty. Migrants were also given a cup but said they had no way to wash it.

Some were also only scheduled to shower three days a week, and the report includes photos of the showers covered in bugs.

images.caption: A bus exits the “Alligator Alcatraz” immigration detention center in the Florida Everglades on May 26, 2026, in Ochopee, Fla.

articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday backed the use of Flock cameras, a controversial surveillance tool .

“Speaking of [artificial intelligence], Flock cameras. You haven’t talked a lot about these Flock cameras. A lot of law enforcement say they really help them. Would you be willing to back that?” a reporter asked Trump on Air Force One.

“No, I sort of like them because of that, because of law enforcement. But some people don’t. They think it’s an infringement,” the president responded , adding later, “I like them.”

Pushback to the AI vehicle surveillance systems operated by Flock Safety has grown on both sides of the aisle.

Flock has a system of license plate readers, video cameras and audio detection devices incorporated into its AI database. That database logs license plate numbers, as well as car features like make, model, color and bumper stickers. Local jurisdictions can share data with other law enforcement agencies, creating a major network that law enforcement can use in crime solving.

Earlier this month, Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who has been on the president’s bad side in the last few years , unveiled a bill aimed at limiting federal funds used for automated license plate reader cameras (ALPRs) and biometric surveillance cameras.

The legislation, named the Flock-Off Act , would halt any effort to buy, install, maintain, operate or upgrade ALPRs and biometric surveillance cameras for municipalities or local law enforcement.

“Federal taxpayers should not be forced to fund the surveillance state,” Massie said in a post on the social platform X, in which he discussed the bill.
